title: Kalidasa's Dynasty of Raghu — the Sanskrit text
author: kalidasa
attributionNote: The mahākāvya of Kālidāsa, the greatest of the Sanskrit poets, who is placed in the fourth or fifth century and connected with the court of the Guptas; the poem follows the kings of the solar dynasty from Dilipa to Agnivarṇa and was commented on by Mallinātha, whose commentary fixed its place in the schools. GRETIL's e-text follows the vocabulary of the Kalidasa Lexicon of A. Scharpé (Brugge 1964).
description: The Raghuvaṃśa tells the solar dynasty in nineteen sargas: Dilipa and the cow of fortune, Raghu's conquest of the world and his sacrifice, Aja and the theft of Indumatī at her own marriage, Dasharatha and the birth of the four brothers, Rama's youth, Sita's abduction, the war with Lanka and the return to Ayodhya, and then the later kings down to Agnivarṇa's corruption — the book in which Kālidāsa answers the epic by telling its family as a poem, and the model of the mahākāvya for a thousand years of Sanskrit court poetry.
historicalContext: Composed in the golden age of the Gupta court, the poem's verses on the seasons, on love in separation and on the duty of the king were imitated by Bhavabhūti, Rājaśekhara and the whole later tradition; it is the work through which the classical Sanskrit poem was defined, and its ninth sarga on the hunt was a school text for a millennium.
availabilityNote: Complete as GRETIL publishes it: all nineteen sargas and 1,637 verses, streamed from GRETIL at read time, one sarga at a time. This is the original Sanskrit, not a translation.
